title: From Baselines to Transport Geodesics: Axiomatic Attribution via Optimal Generative Flows
claim: Our method yields spatially coherent attributions, while baseline attribution methods produce noisy or scattered, high-frequency saliency maps.
layout: 2 rows by 7 columns, left-to-right, ours highlighted in bold final column
description: A 2x7 grid of qualitative saliency heatmaps. Rows are datasets: CIFAR-10 (a low-resolution dog image) on top and CelebA-HQ (a portrait of a man) on the bottom. The first column shows the original image. The next six columns show heatmaps overlaid on the image, one per attribution method: GuidedBackprop, GradientSHAP, IG, SmoothGrad, DDIM and Transport Flow (Ours). The method names are column headers, and the Ours header is in bold. The heatmaps use a jet colormap, with red for high attribution and blue for low. Baseline maps look patchy, scattered or noisy. The Transport Flow maps show smoother, more compact regions on the dog's head and the face's eyes and nose. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmaps and the bold rightmost column.
caption: Qualitative visualization on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-HQ. Transport Flow explanations are spatially coherent and avoid some high-frequency artifacts of straight-line Integrated Gradients. The figure should be read together with Table [ref]; visual clarity alone is not a complete faithfulness metric.
abstract: Feature attributions often hide a critical modeling choice: they explain a prediction along a counterfactual path from a reference state to an input. Different baselines, interpolations, and generative trajectories define different paths and can therefore produce different explanations. We study this path ambiguity as a modeling problem. Our central question is whether the path can be chosen by a distribution-level transport process, rather than by a hand-designed interpolation or by the sensitivity geometry of the model being explained. We separate attribution into fixed-path credit allocation and path selection. For a fixed path, we prove that the Aumann-Shapley line integral is the unique attribution rule under fixed-path axioms and coordinate-trace separability. For path selection, we minimize kinetic action over flows that transport a reference distribution to the data distribution, yielding a transport-geodesic attribution principle. We instantiate this framework using Rectified Flow and derive stability bounds quantifying how vector-field approximation errors affect the resulting attributions. Experiments show that Reflow improves cross-seed attribution stability, while learned transport paths yield spatially coherent explanations with competitive deletion faithfulness among the evaluated path-based methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/cenweizhang/OTFlowSHAP.
